With `site*` or `site?` and a sibling directory that also matches, it returns `invalid result from inner fsys Glob`. The same happens with `os.DirFS`, where `template.ParseFS(sub, \"*.tmpl\")` fails with `pattern matches no files`.\n\n### What did you expect to see?\n\n```\nGlob: [\"index.tmpl\"], <nil>\n```\n\n[`subFS.Glob`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/edd77e8488f86768ab479ba7f03a597bff4a867d/src/io/fs/sub.go#L150) prepends the directory name to the pattern without escaping it, so `path.Match` treats the name as a pattern. The generic `fs.Glob` (used when the `GlobFS` method is not available) returns the expected result for the same Sub. `testing/fstest.TestFS`, which also exercises `fs.Sub`, reports it too: for a `MapFS` with `d[1/hello.txt` and `dz/hello.txt` it fails with `testing fs.Sub(fsys, d[1): Glob(`*a*`): syntax error in pattern`.\n",

    "body": "Fixes #70046. Also affects burrowers/garble#572.\n\nThe go command decides whether to use a response file from the executable\nname. With -toolexec, that name belongs to the wrapper, so compile and\nlink invocations can cross the Windows command-line limit despite the Go\ntools supporting response files.\n\nFor long wrapped Go-tool commands, keep the wrapper arguments and the Go\ntool path on the command line. Put the tool arguments into a response\nfile. Short wrapped commands remain unchanged, including the build\nfarms random response-file exercise. Wrappers that inspect arguments\nmust expand @file before inspecting or modifying tool arguments. Garble\nwill need that adaptation separately.\n\nI added tests for long and short wrapped commands and response-file\nargument fidelity. gofmt and git diff --check passed. I could not run\nthe Go tests yet: the full toolchain bootstrap stalled under this\ncontainers concurrent build load and process limit. This PR is a draft\nuntil the Go test suite and Windows behavior have been checked.\n\nImplemented by Hermes Agent using gpt-6-sol, acting on behalf of @luantak.",

    "body": "### Go version\n\ngo version go1.27.1 linux/amd64 (also go1.26.0, go1.26.3 and go1.26.8; go1.25.5 is not affected)\n\n### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:\n\n```shell\nAR='ar'\nCC='gcc'\nCGO_CFLAGS='-O2 -g'\nCGO_CPPFLAGS=''\nCGO_CXXFLAGS='-O2 -g'\nCGO_ENABLED='0'\nCGO_FFLAGS='-O2 -g'\nCGO_LDFLAGS='-O2 -g'\nCXX='g++'\nGCCGO='gccgo'\nGO111MODULE=''\nGOAMD64='v1'\nGOARCH='amd64'\nGOAUTH='netrc'\nGOBIN='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/go/bin'\nGOCACHE='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/.cache/go-build'\nGOCACHEPROG=''\nGODEBUG=''\nGOENV='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/.config/go/env'\nGOEXE=''\nGOEXPERIMENT=''\nGOFIPS140='off'\nGOFLAGS=''\nGOGCCFLAGS='-fPIC -m64 -Wl,--no-gc-sections -fmessage-length=0 -ffile-prefix-map=/tmp/go-build2312301903=/tmp/go-build -gno-record-gcc-switches'\nGOHOSTARCH='amd64'\nGOHOSTOS='linux'\nGOINSECURE=''\nGOMOD='/dev/null'\nGOMODCACHE='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/go/pkg/mod'\nGONOPROXY=''\nGONOSUMDB=''\nGOOS='linux'\nGOPACKAGESDRIVER=''\nGOPATH='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/go'\nGOPRIVATE=''\nGOPROXY='https://proxy.golang.org,direct'\nGOROOT='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.27.1.linux-amd64'\nGOSUMDB='sum.golang.org'\nGOTELEMETRY='on'\nGOTELEMETRYDIR='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/.config/go/telemetry'\nGOTMPDIR=''\nGOTOOLCHAIN='go1.27.1'\nGOTOOLDIR='/nfs/users/nfs_s/sb10/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.27.1.linux-amd64/pkg/tool/linux_amd64'\nGOVCS=''\nGOVERSION='go1.27.1'\nGOWORK=''\nPKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'\n```\n\n### What did you do?\n\nThe program below runs as three processes. The first process (the watcher) makes two FIFOs, `req` and `rep`. It then re-execs itself as a Go \"server\" and as a \"feeder\":\n\n- The server opens both FIFOs with blocking `syscall.Open`, so the fds are not in the netpoller. It starts 4 goroutines that each loop on `syscall.Read(req, 1 byte)` and then `syscall.Write(rep, 1 byte)`. The main goroutine runs `for { runtime.GC() }`.\n- The feeder writes 1 byte to `req`, then blocks reading the 1-byte reply from `rep`, and repeats. It prints a line every 1000 round trips.\n- The watcher reads the feeder's output. If no line arrives for 5s it prints `HUNG`; if 30s pass without a stall it prints `OK`. It then kills the server and feeder process group and removes the FIFOs.\n\nThe feeder only writes the next byte after the server replies, so at most one reader goroutine has data at a time. The other readers stay blocked in read(2) for as long as the server is stalled.\n\nRun it with `go run main.go`. Setting `GOTRACEBACK=all` makes the watcher send SIGQUIT to the hung server before killing it, so the goroutine dump goes to stderr.\n\nHost: Ubuntu 22.04, Linux 5.15.0-153-generic x86_64, 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon Skylake).\n\n```go\n// Command stwhang shows a stop-the-world that never completes while\n// goroutines sit in blocking read(2) calls on a FIFO that another process\n// writes to only after it gets a reply.\n//\n// Run with no arguments. It re-execs itself twice: as the Go server under\n// test, and as the feeder. The original process watches the feeder's progress\n// and prints one verdict line.\npackage main\n\nimport (\n\t\"bufio\"\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"os/exec\"\n\t\"path/filepath\"\n\t\"runtime\"\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"syscall\"\n\t\"time\"\n)\n\nconst (\n\treaders  = 4\n\tduration = 30 * time.Second\n\tstall    = 5 * time.Second\n)\n\nfunc main() {\n\tif len(os.Args) == 3 {\n\t\tswitch os.Args[1] {\n\t\tcase \"server\":\n\t\t\tserver(os.Args[2])\n\t\tcase \"feeder\":\n\t\t\tfeeder(os.Args[2])\n\t\t}\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tos.Exit(watch())\n}\n\n// server blocks readers goroutines in read(2) on dir/req, replies to each\n// byte on dir/rep, and runs the GC back to back.\nfunc server(dir string) {\n\treq := must(syscall.Open(filepath.Join(dir, \"req\"), syscall.O_RDONLY, 0))\n\trep := must(syscall.Open(filepath.Join(dir, \"rep\"), syscall.O_WRONLY, 0))\n\tfor i := 0; i < readers; i++ {\n\t\tgo func() {\n\t\t\tbuf := make([]byte, 1)\n\t\t\tfor {\n\t\t\t\tif n, err := syscall.Read(req, buf); err == syscall.EINTR {\n\t\t\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t\t\t} else if n != 1 {\n\t\t\t\t\tpanic(fmt.Sprint(\"read: \", n, err))\n\t\t\t\t}\n\t\t\t\tmust(syscall.Write(rep, buf))\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}()\n\t}\n\tfor {\n\t\truntime.GC()\n\t}\n}\n\n// feeder writes one byte to dir/req, waits for the one-byte reply on dir/rep,\n// and prints a line every 1000 round trips.\nfunc feeder(dir string) {\n\treq := must(syscall.Open(filepath.Join(dir, \"req\"), syscall.O_WRONLY, 0))\n\trep := must(syscall.Open(filepath.Join(dir, \"rep\"), syscall.O_RDONLY, 0))\n\tbuf := []byte{'x'}\n\tfor i := 1; ; i++ {\n\t\tmust(syscall.Write(req, buf))\n\t\tif n := must(syscall.Read(rep, buf)); n != 1 {\n\t\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t\t}\n\t\tif i%1000 == 0 {\n\t\t\tfmt.Println(i)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n}\n\n// watch starts the server and feeder, and reports HUNG if the feeder makes\n// no progress for the stall period.\nfunc watch() int {\n\tdir := must(os.MkdirTemp(\"\", \"stwhang\"))\n\tdefer os.RemoveAll(dir)\n\tfor _, name := range []string{\"req\", \"rep\"} {\n\t\tmust(0, syscall.Mkfifo(filepath.Join(dir, name), 0o600))\n\t}\n\n\tsrv := exec.Command(os.Args[0], \"server\", dir)\n\tsrv.Stderr = os.Stderr\n\tsrv.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true}\n\tmust(0, srv.Start())\n\n\tfdr := exec.Command(os.Args[0], \"feeder\", dir)\n\tfdr.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true, Pgid: srv.Process.Pid}\n\tout := must(fdr.StdoutPipe())\n\tmust(0, fdr.Start())\n\tdefer func() { // kill the server and feeder process group, then reap both\n\t\tsyscall.Kill(-srv.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGKILL)\n\t\tsrv.Wait()\n\t\tfdr.Wait()\n\t}()\n\n\tprogress := make(chan string)\n\tgo func() {\n\t\tfor sc := bufio.NewScanner(out); sc.Scan(); {\n\t\t\tprogress <- sc.Text()\n\t\t}\n\t\tclose(progress)\n\t}()\n\n\tlast, end := \"0\", time.After(duration)\n\tfor {\n\t\tselect {\n\t\tcase p, ok := <-progress:\n\t\t\tif !ok {\n\t\t\t\tfmt.Printf(\"ERROR: feeder exited after %s round trips\\n\", last)\n\t\t\t\treturn 2\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tlast = p\n\t\tcase <-time.After(stall):\n\t\t\tfmt.Printf(\"HUNG: %s: no progress for %s after %s round trips; server threads (wchan/state): %s\\n\",\n\t\t\t\truntime.Version(), stall, last, threads(srv.Process.Pid))\n\t\t\tif os.Getenv(\"GOTRACEBACK\") != \"\" {\n\t\t\t\tsyscall.Kill(srv.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGQUIT)\n\t\t\t\ttime.Sleep(2 * time.Second)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\treturn 1\n\t\tcase <-end:\n\t\t\tfmt.Printf(\"OK: %s: %s round trips in %s, no hang\\n\", runtime.Version(), last, duration)\n\t\t\treturn 0\n\t\t}\n\t}\n}\n\n// threads counts the server's threads by kernel wait channel and state.\nfunc threads(pid int) string {\n\tcounts := map[string]int{}\n\ttasks, _ := filepath.Glob(fmt.Sprintf(\"/proc/%d/task/*\", pid))\n\tfor _, task := range tasks {\n\t\twchan, _ := os.ReadFile(task + \"/wchan\")\n\t\tstat, _ := os.ReadFile(task + \"/stat\")\n\t\tstate := \"?\"\n\t\tif f := strings.Fields(string(stat)); len(f) > 2 {\n\t\t\tstate = f[2]\n\t\t}\n\t\tcounts[string(wchan)+\"/\"+state]++\n\t}\n\treturn fmt.Sprint(counts)\n}\n\nfunc must[T any](v T, err error) T {\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\tpanic(err)\n\t}\n\treturn v\n}\n```\n\n### What did you see happen?\n\nOn go1.26 and go1.27 the server stops replying, after anywhere from 1,000 to 307,000 round trips in these runs. It never recovers:\n\n```\n$ go run main.go\nHUNG: go1.27.1: no progress for 5s after 101000 round trips; server threads (wchan/state): map[futex_wait_queue_me/S:11 pipe_read/S:3]\n```\n\nHung runs per version, 30s per run (blank: not tried):\n\n| Version | default (8 CPUs) | GODEBUG=asyncpreemptoff=1 | GOMAXPROCS=1 | GOMAXPROCS=2 | GOMAXPROCS=8 |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| go1.25.5 | 0/10 | 0/5 | 0/5 | 0/5 | 0/5 |\n| go1.26.0 | 10/10 | | | | |\n| go1.26.3 | 10/10 | 5/5 | 0/5 | 4/5 | 5/5 |\n| go1.26.8 | 10/10 | | | | |\n| go1.27.1 | 10/10 | 5/5 | 0/5 | 4/5 | 5/5 |\n\nIn every hung run the server's threads were in the same kernel state, read from `/proc/<pid>/task/*/{wchan,stat}`: 3 threads sleeping in `pipe_read` and all the others in `futex_wait_queue_me`. In a few runs, one thread was also running (wchan 0, state R). The one reader that got the feeder's last byte has left read(2), but its reply never arrives. The feeder is blocked in `pipe_read` on `rep`.\n\nThe SIGQUIT dump (go1.27.1, trimmed to the relevant goroutines) shows a mark-termination stop-the-world in progress. The reader that returned from read(2) is `[runnable]` and has no M, and no goroutine is running. Goroutines 20 and 22 are the same as goroutine 19: `[syscall]`, each still on an M. The other goroutines in the dump are idle GC workers, the finalizer, the sweeper, the scavenger, and a second mark worker in `semacquire` inside `gcMarkDone`.\n\n```\ngoroutine 1 gp=0x10a627a101e0 m=nil [wait for GC cycle]:\nruntime.gopark(0x10a627a9ecf0?, 0x10a627a52000?, 0x0?, 0x0?, 0x0?)\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/proc.go:474 +0xca\nruntime.goparkunlock(...)\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/proc.go:480\nruntime.gcWaitOnMark(0x19d2)\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:663 +0x5b\nruntime.GC()\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:558 +0x45\nmain.server({0x7ffec3f40823, 0xa9})\n\tmain.go:60 +0x136\nmain.main()\n\tmain.go:32 +0x66\nruntime.main()\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427\nruntime.goexit({})\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1\n\ngoroutine 19 gp=0x10a627b823c0 m=10 mp=0x10a627b01808 [syscall]:\nsyscall.Syscall(0x0, 0x5, 0x10a627a75777, 0x1)\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/syscall_linux.go:74 +0x25\nsyscall.read(0x5?, {0x10a627a75777?, 0x1?, 0x1?})\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/zsyscall_linux_amd64.go:736 +0x38\nsyscall.Read(...)\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/syscall_unix.go:183\nmain.server.func1()\n\tmain.go:50 +0x46\nruntime.goexit({})\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1\ncreated by main.server in goroutine 1\n\tmain.go:47 +0x11e\n\ngoroutine 21 gp=0x10a627b82780 m=nil [runnable]:\nsyscall.Syscall(0x0, 0x5, 0x10a627a76777, 0x1)\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/syscall_linux.go:74 +0x25\nsyscall.read(0x6?, {0x10a627a76777?, 0x1?, 0x1?})\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/zsyscall_linux_amd64.go:736 +0x38\nsyscall.Read(...)\n\t$GOROOT/src/syscall/syscall_unix.go:183\nmain.server.func1()\n\tmain.go:50 +0x46\nruntime.goexit({})\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1\ncreated by main.server in goroutine 1\n\tmain.go:47 +0x11e\n\ngoroutine 25 gp=0x10a627b82f00 m=5 mp=0x10a627c00008 [stopping the world]:\nruntime.systemstack_switch()\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:481 +0x8\nruntime.gcMarkDone()\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:1065 +0x21f\nruntime.gcBgMarkWorker(0x10a627b860e0)\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:1928 +0x2c5\nruntime.gcBgMarkStartWorkers.gowrap1()\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:1711 +0x17\nruntime.goexit({})\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1\ncreated by runtime.gcBgMarkStartWorkers in goroutine 1\n\t$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgc.go:1711 +0xfc\n```\n\n### What did you expect to see?\n\nThe program should run for the full 30s and print `OK`, as it does on go1.25.5. Goroutines blocked in a syscall should not stop the stop-the-world from completing. The reader that returned from its syscall should then run and reply.\n\nContext: I found this in a FUSE server built on go-fuse, in [wr](https://github.com/VertebrateResequencing/wr). There, a process blocked on a FUSE request plays the feeder's role, and `/dev/fuse` plays `req`. The program above reproduces the hang without FUSE, cgo or third-party code. It is not #11155: nothing here forks, and no thread is blocked in vfork or chdir.\n\nSuspected area (unverified): go1.26's change to how stop-the-world takes the Ps of goroutines in syscalls (`_Psyscall` removed; `setBlockOnExitSyscall` in runtime/proc.go).\n",

    "body": "### Go version\n\ngo version go1.28-devel_651ec67c3b Fri Sep 25 09:02:19 2026 -0700 (master), building for `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64`. go1.27.1 generates the same code, so this isn't a regression.\n\n### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:\n\n```shell\nGOOS=linux\nGOARCH=arm64\nGOARM64=v8.0\nCGO_ENABLED=0\nGOEXPERIMENT=\n```\n\nCross-compiled from linux/amd64 and benchmarked on linux/arm64 (Neoverse N1).\n\n### What did you do?\n\nA loop multiplying by a 64-bit constant that doesn't fit an arm64 immediate, compared with the same loop loading the constant from a variable:\n\n```go\npackage repro\n\nconst prime = 0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463\n\n//go:noinline\nfunc Hash(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {\n\tfor i, v := range src {\n\t\tdst[i] = uint32((v * prime) >> 45)\n\t}\n}\n\nvar primeVar uint64 = prime\n\n//go:noinline\nfunc HashVar(dst []uint32, src []uint64) {\n\tp := primeVar\n\tfor i, v := range src {\n\t\tdst[i] = uint32((v * p) >> 45)\n\t}\n}\n```\n\n### What did you see happen?\n\n`Hash` rebuilds the constant with `MOVD` + 3×`MOVK` on every iteration, even though the loop uses only a handful of registers. (From `go tool objdump`, with branch targets relabelled for readability.)\n\n```\nloop:\n\tLSR\t$45, R5, R5\n\tMOVW\tR5, (R0)(R2<<2)\n\tADD\t$1, R2, R2\n\tCMP\tR2, R4\n\tBLE\tdone\n\tMOVD\t(R3)(R2<<3), R5\n\tMOVD\t$25699, R6\n\tMOVK\t$(47013<<16), R6\n\tMOVK\t$(48348<<32), R6\n\tMOVK\t$(53019<<48), R6\n\tMUL\tR6, R5, R5\n\tCMP\tR2, R1\n\tBHI\tloop\n```\n\n`HashVar` loads it once before the loop and keeps it in `R2`:\n\n```\n\tADRP\t..., R27\n\tMOVD\t1232(R27), R2\nloop:\n\tLSR\t$45, R6, R6\n\tMOVW\tR6, (R0)(R5<<2)\n\tADD\t$1, R5, R5\n\tCMP\tR5, R4\n\tBLE\tdone\n\tMOVD\t(R3)(R5<<3), R6\n\tMUL\tR2, R6, R6\n\tCMP\tR5, R1\n\tBHI\tloop\n```\n\nOn a Neoverse N1 (4096 elements, one pinned core, `-count 10`), `HashVar` is 20% faster:\n\n```\n     │   Hash    │              HashVar               │\n     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base               │\nHash   5.161µ ± 0%   4.128µ ± 0%  -20.02% (p=0.000 n=10)\n```\n\nFor comparison, amd64 makes the same choice, rebuilding the constant inside the loop, but there it is a single `MOVQ $imm64` with no dependency chain:\n\n```\nloop:\n\tSHRQ\t$0x2d, DX\n\tMOVL\tDX, 0(AX)(CX*4)\n\tINCQ\tCX\n\tCMPQ\tSI, CX\n\tJLE\tdone\n\tMOVQ\t0(DI)(CX*8), DX\n\tMOVQ\t$0xcf1bbcdcb7a56463, R8\n\tIMULQ\tR8, DX\n\tCMPQ\tBX, CX\n\tJA\tloop\n```\n\nso the same comparison on a Ryzen 5 5600X is much smaller:\n\n```\n     │   Hash    │              HashVar              │\n     │  sec/op   │   sec/op     vs base              │\nHash   2.037µ ± 7%   1.956µ ± 2%  -3.98% (p=0.000 n=10)\n```\n\n### What did you expect to see?\n\nThe constant built once outside the loop and kept in a register, as with `HashVar`.\n\nAs far as I can tell, this is because `MOVDconst` is marked `rematerializeable: true` ([ARM64Ops.go#L413](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/_gen/ARM64Ops.go#L413)), and [`(*Value).Rematerializeable`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/651ec67c3b79c44100276c0666339c8ba1d7f727/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssa/regalloc.go#L165) only looks at the opcode. So the register allocator treats a constant that takes 4 instructions to build the same as one that takes 1. That's the right call on amd64, where `MOVQ $imm64` is always one instruction, but not on arm64. The `MOVDconst` ops for riscv64, ppc64, mips64 and loong64 carry the same flag. I haven't checked their code generation.\n\nMotivation: this showed up in the zstd encoder's match-finder hashing in klauspost/compress. https://github.com/klauspost/compress/pull/1230 works around it by loading the hash primes from a package-level `var` on arm64 only (`hashPrimesInRegs = runtime.GOARCH == \"arm64\"`). That accounts for most of the PR's +6–8% encode throughput on Graviton2/3/4. On amd64 the same workaround is slower, because rebuilding the constant costs a single `MOVQ` and holding it adds spills in a loop that already has high register pressure. So the workaround has to be per-architecture, and it would be better fixed in the compiler.\n\nLoop-invariant code motion (#63670) wouldn't help on its own: SSA constants already live in the entry block, outside the loop, and the register allocator re-emits them at each use.\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n",

    "body": "A common mistake often (but not always) flagged during code review is to return (i.e. read from) a variable in the same statement that populates (i.e. writes to) the result variable, for example:\n\n```go\nfunc f(input string) (Result, err)\n   var res Result\n   return res, res.parse(input)\n}\n\nfunc (*Result) parse(string) error { ... }\n```\n\nThe behavior of this program is not specified. The compiler is free to compile the load of res before or after the call to parse. The current compiler tends to make the call first, so the load observes its effect, as the code author presumably intended. But a different compiler (such as one based on x/tools/go/ssa) computes the load first, so the function always returns a zero value, even when `parse` successfully mutated the variable.\n\n@ianlancetaylor suggested that `vet` might flag such mistakes. I did a quick experiment with a prototype analyzer (https://go.dev/cl/836485) written by a coding agent that looks for exactly the narrow pattern above. At least half, and perhaps 80%, of its findings (a sample of which are listed below) appear to be genuine bugs, so there is promise here. However, the number of false positives is too high, and the pattern is too specific, as there are undoubtedly other forms of this mistake that we could catch.\n\nIn other words, this is promising but further research is needed.\n\n--\n\nHere's a sample of 25 of 171 findings across 16K modules.     "body": "### Proposal\n\nAdd a username-aware rejection hook to `ssh.ServerConfig`:\n\n```go\nPreAuthUserCallback func(ConnMetadata) error\n```\n\nThe hook runs before processing each authentication request, including the initial `none` request. Returning nil continues normal authentication. Returning an error disconnects the client with `SSH_DISCONNECT_HOST_NOT_ALLOWED_TO_CONNECT` (reason 1) and a fixed message. The application receives the error through `ServerAuthError`; its text is not sent to the client.\n\n### Why\n\nAn SFTP server with per-user IP allowlists needs the requested username to choose the allowlist, but should reject a disallowed source address before offering password authentication. Checking in `PasswordCallback` happens after the client has already supplied a password.\n\n`PreAuthConnCallback` runs before the username is available. `NoClientAuthCallback` requires enabling `NoClientAuth` and only handles `none` requests; clients can skip those. `BannerCallback` runs once and cannot return a rejection error. Closing a captured network connection from that callback is possible, but does not provide this per-request check and SSH disconnect response.\n\n### Behavior and compatibility\n\n- Leaving the hook nil preserves existing behavior. Returning nil does not authenticate anyone or change the offered methods.\n- Check every request because clients can change usernames before partial authentication succeeds, repeat requests, or send credentials without a `none` probe.\n- The username is a client claim, not an authenticated identity. Applications must consider whether their allow/deny responses reveal account existence.\n- Expensive policy checks run before authentication and may repeat; the application remains responsible for their cost.\n\nThis proposal lets a server reject a connection before processing authentication; it does not select authentication methods. The earlier banner and multi-step-authentication proposals address different needs: #68688 and #64974.\n\nImplementation: https://github.com/golang/crypto/pull/376\n",

    "body": "When a client connection goes away, a handler blocked in Write or\nBody.Read gets an error, but r.Context().Err() can still be nil at\nthat point. teardown closes doneServing, which wakes up handlers\nwaiting to write, before closeAllStreamsOnConnClose cancels the stream\ncontexts. Similarly, when a frame write fails, wroteFrame passes the\nerror back to the handler, and nothing cancels the contexts until the\nserve loop notices the closed connection and runs teardown.\n\nThe HTTP/1 server cancels the connection's context before it returns\na read or write error to the handler. Do the same here: cancel the\nbase context, which every stream context derives from, before teardown\ncloses doneServing and before wroteFrame reports a failed write.\n\nFixes #52183\n",

    "body": "`net.IPMask.MarshalText` gained a new text format in the Go 1.28 cycle (issue #29678), gated behind `GODEBUG=netmarshal=1`. For a mask whose length is not 0, 4, or 16 bytes, the new path returns empty bytes with a nil error instead of an error, and the data is silently destroyed:\n\n```go\nm := net.IPMask{255, 255, 255, 0, 1}\nb, err := m.MarshalText()  // GODEBUG=netmarshal=1: b=\"\", err=nil\nj, _ := json.Marshal(m)    // j = \"\"\nvar m2 net.IPMask\njson.Unmarshal(j, &m2)     // m2 = [] -- the original 5 bytes are gone\n```\n\n(The old base64 format round-trips the same mask fine.)\n\nRoot cause in `src/net/ip.go`:\n\n```go\naddr, _ := netip.AddrFromSlice(m)\nreturn addr.AppendTo(nil), nil\n```\n\nThe `ok` result is discarded; on failure `addr` is the zero `Addr` and `AppendTo(nil)` yields nothing. The sibling `IP.MarshalText` returns an honest error (`address 0102030405: invalid IP address`) for invalid lengths, so this is also internally inconsistent. The existing `ipMaskJSONTests` table only covers nil/4-byte/16-byte masks, which is why it slipped through.\n\nExpected: `MarshalText` returns a non-nil error for a mask that cannot be represented as an IP address.\n\nSeen on master at `8190b02c` (2026-09-25), linux/amd64, go1.28-devel.",

    "body": "This fixes #81605.\n\n**What was happening:** `root.Mkdir(\"parent/rooted\", ...)` failed with `permission denied` when `parent` had mode `0300` (write and search, but no read), while the equivalent `os.Mkdir` succeeded. I reproduced this on Linux as an unprivileged user: creating an entry in a directory only needs write+search permission on it, but `os.Root` was additionally demanding read permission on every intermediate directory. The reporter's analysis nailed the cause: `rootOpenDir` opens intermediates without `O_PATH`, so the open is a read-only open.\n\n**The fix:** on Linux, open intermediate directories with `O_PATH` (new `rootOpenDirFlags` constant, `O_PATH` on Linux and 0 elsewhere so other platforms are untouched). An `O_PATH` open needs no access mode on the directory itself, and O_PATH descriptors work fine as the dirfd for all the `*at` calls made relative to intermediate directories. Symlink handling is unchanged: with `O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY`, opening a symlink fails with `ENOTDIR`, which the existing `checkSymlink` path already turns into `errSymlink` for safe in-root resolution. I verified the symlink behavior of the flag combination directly against the kernel before relying on it.\n\nOne subtlety I caught while testing: `os.RemoveAll` also opens directories through `openDirAt`, and an `O_PATH` descriptor cannot be readdir'd, so a blanket change broke `RemoveAll` (its temp-dir cleanup started failing). The open is now factored into `openDirNoFollow` taking extra flags: `rootOpenDir` passes `O_PATH` on Linux, while `RemoveAll` gets `openReadableDir`, which keeps the previous read-only open. `RemoveAll` behavior is unchanged on every platform.\n\n**Tests:** added `TestRootNoReadPermission`, which exercises `Mkdir`, `MkdirAll`, `Create`, `Stat`, `Symlink`, and `Readlink` beneath a `0300` directory (skipped on non-Linux and when run as root, following the existing convention in the os tests). Verified the reproducer from the issue now prints `<nil>` for both `os.Mkdir` and `Root.Mkdir`, verified `os.RemoveAll` still works, and ran the `os` package's root tests.",

    "body": "This fixes #81632.\n\n**What was happening:** compiling a file with a raw NUL byte inside a string literal succeeded silently, but only when the NUL happened to be the first byte read after the scanner's buffer was refilled (in my testing, at offsets 8190 and 16382 into the literal, and the reporter's comment confirms the pattern at every buffer doubling). `gofmt` and `go vet` both reject the same file with \"illegal character NUL\", so the compiler accepting it was clearly a miss.\n\n**Why:** in `(*source).nextch` (`src/cmd/compile/internal/syntax/source.go`), only the ASCII fast path checked for NUL. The general path refills the buffer and decodes with `utf8.DecodeRune`, which decodes a lone NUL byte without complaint, and nothing checked for it afterwards.\n\n**The fix:** mirror the fast path's NUL check in the general path.\n\n**Tests:** added `TestIssue81632`, which puts a NUL at several offsets including the buffer-refill boundaries. I verified it fails without the fix (no error reported at 4075/8190/16382) and passes with it, and ran the full `cmd/compile/internal/syntax` package suite, all green.",

      "html_url": "https://github.com/golang/go/pull/81746",
      "diff_url": "https://github.com/golang/go/pull/81746.diff",
      "patch_url": "https://github.com/golang/go/pull/81746.patch",
      "merged_at": null
    },
    "body": "Hi, I ran into this while testing `http.ServeContent` with a client that sends a non-standard range unit.\n\n**What was happening:** sending `Range: items=0-3` (or any unit other than `bytes`) made `ServeContent` respond `416 Requested Range Not Satisfiable` with the body \"invalid range\". Per RFC 7233, Section 3.1, an origin server MUST ignore a Range header field containing a range unit it does not understand, so the expected behavior is to serve the full content with a 200.\n\n**Reproduction:**\n\n```go\nreq := httptest.NewRequest(\"GET\", \"/\", nil)\nreq.Header.Set(\"Range\", \"items=0-3\")\nrec := httptest.NewRecorder()\nhttp.ServeContent(rec, req, \"test.txt\", time.Now(), strings.NewReader(\"0123456789\"))\n// before: 416, body \"invalid range\\n\"\n// after:  200, body \"0123456789\"\n```\n\n**The fix:** in `parseRange` (`src/net/http/fs.go`), when the header does not start with `bytes=`, return `(nil, nil)` instead of an \"invalid range\" error, treating the header as not present. Malformed `bytes` ranges (e.g. `bytes=5-4`, `bytes=A-`) still return 416 as before, since those are genuinely invalid byte-range specifiers.\n\n**Tests:**\n- Added `TestParseRangeIgnoresUnknownRangeUnit` (`src/net/http/range_test.go`): asserts `parseRange` returns `(nil, nil)` for `items=0-3`, `ITEMS=0-3`, `pages=1-2`, `bytes2=0-3`, and `foo`.\n- Added `TestServeContentIgnoresUnknownRangeUnit` (`src/net/http/fs_test.go`): asserts `ServeContent` returns 200 with the full body for unknown range units.\n- Verified both new tests fail on unpatched master (416 + \"invalid range\") and pass with the fix.\n- Ran the full `net/http` package suite: all green except a pre-existing `TestTransportRequestWriteRoundTrip` h3 subtest failure (QUIC handshake timeout in this environment), which fails identically on unpatched master.\n\nFixes #81508.\n",

    "body": "The cpu.max interface file is only present in cgroup v2 when the kernel is built with CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH, even if the cpu controller is enabled in the parent's cgroup.subtree_control. Without it, SetCPUMax tries to create the file, which cgroupfs rejects with EACCES, and TestInCgroupV2 fails with:\r\n\r\n  Erroring setting cpu.max: open /sys/fs/cgroup/go-cgrouptestNNN/cpu.max: permission denied\r\n\r\nSkip, like the other best-effort checks in InCgroupV2, when the new cgroup does not have cpu.max.\r\n\r\nThis PR will be imported into Gerrit with the title and first\r\ncomment (this text) used to generate the subject and body of\r\nthe Gerrit change.\r\n\r\n**Please ensure you adhere to every item in this list.**\r\n\r\nMore info can be found at https://go.dev/wiki/CommitMessage\r\n\r\n+ The PR title is formatted as follows: `net/http: frob the quux before blarfing`\r\n  + The package name goes before the colon\r\n  + The part after the colon uses the verb tense + phrase that completes the blank in,\r\n    \"This change modifies Go to ___________\"\r\n  + Lowercase verb after the colon\r\n  + No trailing period\r\n  + Keep the title as short as possible, ideally 72 characters or shorter\r\n+ No Markdown\r\n+ The first PR comment (this one) is wrapped at around 72 characters, unless it's\r\n  really needed (ASCII art, table, or long link)\r\n+ If there is a corresponding issue, add either `Fixes #1234` or `Updates #1234`\r\n  (the latter if this is not a complete fix) to this comment\r\n+ If referring to a repo other than `golang/go` you can use the\r\n  `owner/repo#issue_number` syntax: `Fixes golang/vscode-go#1234`\r\n+ We do not use Signed-off-by lines in Go. Please don't add them.\r\n  Our Gerrit server & GitHub bots enforce CLA compliance instead.\r\n+ Delete these instructions once you have read and applied them\r\n",
